content.lab-rule-zero.title: Pick well
content.lab-rule-zero.tagline: Look past the spark to the person you would build a life with.
content.lab-rule-zero.description: Most marriages that struggle were decided long before the first argument — at the choosing. Work through four situations together and notice what each of you weighs, and what you overlook.
content.lab-rule-zero.cover.alt: Two cups of tea on a café table in late afternoon light.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-intro.title: Attraction starts it. Character carries it.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-intro.body: Feeling drawn to someone matters — it is part of a good match. But it fades and returns in waves, while character, deen, values and how someone handles stress show up every single day. This lesson is about seeing both clearly.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.title: The charming one
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.body: Imran is funny, confident and easy to talk to. In three meetings he has been late twice, spoke sharply to a waiter, and changed the subject whenever prayer came up.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.prompt: What do you make of it?
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.image.alt: A charming man laughing while a waiter looks uncomfortable.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.choices.chem: The chemistry is rare — the rest will settle once we are married.
Two years in, the lateness is constant and the sharpness is now aimed at you when he is stressed. Chemistry did not change him; it made the early signs easy to forgive.
Ask him directly about the waiter and about prayer, and watch how he answers.
He could laugh it off, get defensive, or reflect honestly. Whichever he does, you now know how he responds to a gentle challenge — which is how he will respond in marriage.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.choices.fami: Let my family meet him and see what they notice.
Your uncle notices the same edge you did. Others who care about you can see what attraction blurs — though their view helps most alongside your own questions, not instead of them.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-charm.choices.walk: End it now — those are red flags.
You may be right. You may also have ended something over a bad week without asking a single question. Clear standards are good; deciding without understanding can cost you a good person.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-list.title: The list
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-list.image.alt: A young woman revising a handwritten list.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-list.body: Sana has a list: tall, a doctor or engineer, from her community, lives in London. Hamza meets none of these. He is steady, kind, prays on time, and talks openly about wanting a calm home.
Hold to the list. She knows what she wants.
She waits three more years for someone who ticks every box — and finds the boxes said little about whether they could live together kindly.
Split the list into must-haves and nice-to-haves, then look again.
Deen, kindness and wanting the same kind of home move to the top. Height and job title move down. Hamza suddenly looks like a serious possibility.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-list.choices.settl: Forget the list — any good Muslim will do.
Abandoning every preference can lead to resentment later. Some things on her list — like where she lives — might genuinely matter. Sorting is better than discarding.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-money.title: The question nobody asks
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-money.image.alt: A couple looking at a notebook of sums together.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-money.body: Yusuf and Mariam are getting on wonderfully. Neither has asked about debt, spending, supporting parents, or who works after children arrive. It feels unromantic to bring it up.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-money.choices.afte: After the nikah. Talking money now would spoil it.
Three months in, Mariam learns Yusuf sends half his salary to his parents and has a car loan. Nothing about it is wrong — but finding out now feels like being misled.
Now, kindly and plainly, before anyone is too attached.
It is awkward for ten minutes. Then they learn they both expect to support parents, and agree on how. It becomes the conversation that made them trust each other.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-money.choices.fami: Let the families sort it out.
The families agree a mahr and a wedding budget. Day-to-day money — habits, debts, priorities — never gets discussed, and that is where the arguments come from.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.title: The bad day
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.image.alt: A tired young man apologising to a guard on a train platform.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.body: On a long delayed train journey with a chaperone, you see the person you are considering at the end of their patience: tired, hungry, plans ruined.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.choices.per: That they stay perfectly calm. Anything else is a warning.
Nobody stays perfectly calm. Expecting it means anyone real will disappoint you — the question is how someone is when they are not at their best.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.choices.how: How they treat people when frustrated, and whether they recover.
They grumble, then apologise to the guard they snapped at and make a joke of it. That repair is exactly what you will need in a marriage.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-stress.choices.ign: Nothing — everyone is different on a bad day.
Bad days are where marriage actually happens. Treating them as not counting means missing the most honest information you will get before the nikah.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.title: What to actually look at
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.body: Attraction is a reason to keep talking. These decide whether a marriage holds:
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.points.0: Deen you can share, not just a label you both use
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.points.1: Character under pressure — how they treat people who can do nothing for them
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.points.2: Emotional maturity: can they apologise, listen, and repair
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.points.3: Values and expectations: roles, money, children, family, where you live
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-insight.points.4: Whether your families can become one family
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-talk.prompt: Name one thing each of you would never compromise on — and one thing you used to think mattered but no longer do.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-talk.followUps.0: What did you each notice the other weigh differently in the scenarios?
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-talk.followUps.1: Which question are you most nervous to ask each other?
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-talk.guide.z-g1.te: Ask the unromantic questions early: money, family, children, roles.
content.lab-rule-zero.steps.z-talk.guide.z-g2.te: Judge character by bad days, not good ones.
content.lab-rule-one.title: Sweat the small stuff
content.lab-rule-one.tagline: Small things left unsaid become big things that cannot be.
content.lab-rule-one.description: Resentment rarely starts big. It grows from a dish left out, a comment at dinner, a plan changed without asking. Practise catching small things while they are still small.
content.lab-rule-one.cover.alt: A single mug left beside a kitchen sink.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-intro.title: The pebble and the wall
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-intro.body: Each small irritation you swallow is a pebble. One is nothing. A hundred quietly become a wall — and one day a tiny thing gets a huge reaction, and neither of you understands why.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.title: Dinner and the phone
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.body: Six months married. Most evenings, Adam scrolls his phone through dinner. Layla minds, but it seems petty to say anything — he works hard.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.image.alt: A husband on his phone at dinner while his wife looks away.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.choices.swall: Let it go. It is not worth an argument.
Months later he checks his phone while she tells him about her day, and she explodes. He is baffled — she never said anything. To her, it has been happening for half a year.
Make a pointed joke about him marrying his phone.
He laughs and does not change. Hints let you feel you said something while leaving him free to miss it — and a joke with an edge often lands as criticism.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.choices.say.l: "I miss you at dinner. Could we keep phones away while we eat?"
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-phone.choices.say.c: He had not noticed. He agrees, slips sometimes, and she reminds him gently. A small thing stayed a small thing.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.title: A comment at his mother’s
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.image.alt: A young wife smiling stiffly at a family dinner.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.body: At his mother’s house, she jokes that Layla’s cooking “still needs practice”. Everyone laughs. Layla smiles. Adam does not notice anything wrong.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.prompt: Later, at home, what should Layla do?
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.choices.fine: Say nothing. It was a joke, and it is his mother.
The jokes continue every visit. Layla starts dreading Fridays, then finding reasons not to go. Adam thinks she does not like his family, and resents that.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.choices.atta: "Your mother humiliated me and you just sat there."
Adam defends his mother on instinct. Now they are arguing about loyalty, not about one comment — and the actual hurt never gets heard.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-mother.choices.soft: "The cooking comment stung a bit. Can I tell you why?"
Adam had heard it as nothing. Hearing it calmly, he can see it. Next time he says, “Layla’s biryani is the best I’ve had,” and his mother takes the hint.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.title: Now you are the one hearing it
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.image.alt: A husband turning to listen as his wife speaks.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.body: Your spouse says, quietly: “It bothers me that you always decide our weekend plans without asking.” You did not know. It feels like criticism out of nowhere.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.choices.de: "I only do it because you never suggest anything."
True or not, they learn that raising small things leads to a counter-attack. Next time, they will stay quiet — and the pebbles start piling up.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.choices.th: "Thank you for telling me. What would you like instead?"
They relax. You agree to plan Saturdays together. Because it was easy to say, they will keep telling you small things — which is how you never get big ones.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-receiver.choices.su: It sounds like agreement but lands as punishment. They got the change and lost the warmth. Small things become harder to raise next time.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-insight.title: Why small things are the big things
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-insight.body: Raising something small is only half of it. The other half is making it safe to hear. Couples who do well keep the bar for raising things low, and the reaction to hearing them gentle.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-insight.points.0: Say it within a day or two, while it is still small
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-insight.points.1: Describe what happened and how it felt — not what kind of person they are
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-insight.points.3: When you are told something, thank them first and explain later
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-talk.prompt: What is a small thing that would bother each of you if it kept happening? Say it now, while it is still hypothetical.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-talk.followUps.0: How would you each like to be told when something is bothering the other?
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-talk.guide.o-g1.tex: Bring up small problems early, while they are still small.
content.lab-rule-one.steps.o-talk.guide.o-g2.tex: When one of us raises something, the other says thank you first.
content.lab-rule-two.title: Listen before you defend
content.lab-rule-two.description: When someone you love is upset with you, everything in you wants to explain. Practise the harder thing: asking, acknowledging and validating before you defend.
content.lab-rule-two.cover.alt: One person speaking while the other leans in to listen.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-intro.title: Two conversations at once
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-intro.body: When one person is hurt and the other starts explaining, two conversations happen at once and neither is heard. Listening first is not losing. It is how the conversation becomes one.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.title: Late again
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.body: Zainab: “You said you’d be home for iftar. I broke my fast alone, again.” Omar was stuck in a meeting he could not leave.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.image.alt: A woman alone at an iftar table as her husband arrives late.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.choices.explai: "The meeting overran — there was nothing I could do."
Completely true, and she feels unheard. She was not asking whether it was his fault; she was telling him she felt alone. Now she has to argue to be understood.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.choices.ack.la: "You broke your fast on your own. That must have felt lonely."
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-late.choices.ack.co: Her shoulders drop. A minute later she asks what happened, and he tells her about the meeting. The same explanation lands completely differently after she has been heard.
It ends the conversation fast, which can feel like being brushed off. An apology without understanding often sounds like wanting it to stop.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.title: When it feels unfair
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.image.alt: A wife pausing to listen as her husband talks in frustration.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.body: Ibrahim: “You always take your sister’s side.” Aisha thinks this is simply not true — she sided with him last week.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.choices.corr: Point out last week. “Always” is unfair.
She wins the point about the word and loses the conversation. He walks away believing she cannot even hear him.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.choices.curi: "What happened that made it feel that way?"
It was one moment at dinner when she laughed at her sister’s joke about him. That is much easier to talk about than “always”.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-unfair.choices.agre: "You’re right, I always do. I’m sorry."
Agreeing to something you do not believe builds quiet resentment, and he does not learn what really hurt either. Validation is not surrender.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.title: Validation without agreement
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.image.alt: One spouse kneeling to comfort the other.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.body: Your spouse is upset you told your parents about a disagreement between you. You believe asking your parents for advice was reasonable.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.prompt: Which response validates without giving up your view?
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.choices.ye: "I get why that felt like a betrayal — it was between us. Can I tell you why I did it?"
They feel understood, then genuinely listen to your reasons. You might still disagree, but now you are deciding together what stays private.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.choices.bu: "I understand, but they are my parents and I needed advice."
The “but” erases everything before it. They hear only the defence.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-validate.choices.ov: "You’re overreacting — it’s not a big deal."
Telling someone how big their feelings should be is the fastest way to make them bigger.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.title: Listen, ask, acknowledge — then explain
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.body: Validation means “your feelings make sense”, not “you are right”. You can say it and still disagree.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.points.0: Listen to the end without preparing your answer
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.points.1: Ask one question to understand more
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.points.2: Say back what you heard, in your own words
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-insight.points.4: Only then explain your side — briefly
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-talk.prompt: When you are upset, what do you most need to hear first? And what is the one response that makes it worse?
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-talk.followUps.0: Which of the tempting answers above sounded most like you?
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-talk.guide.t-g1.tex: Listen and acknowledge before explaining or defending.
content.lab-rule-two.steps.t-talk.guide.t-g2.tex: Validation does not mean agreement — we can say both.
content.lab-rule-three.title: The anxious–avoidant loop
content.lab-rule-three.tagline: One reaches out, the other pulls back — and both feel more alone.
content.lab-rule-three.description: When one person feels disconnected they may pursue; when the other feels pressured they may withdraw. Each move makes the other’s worse. Learn to see the loop, and to step out of it together.
content.lab-rule-three.cover.alt: Two figures on a looping path, one reaching, one turning away.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-intro.title: Neither of you is the problem. The loop is.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-intro.body: Some people, when they feel distance, move closer: more messages, more questions. Some, when they feel pressure, move away: quieter, busier, needing space. Neither is wrong. Together they can lock into a loop.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.title: He has gone quiet
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.body: Bilal had a hard week and has been quiet for two days — short replies, early nights. Safiya wonders if she has done something wrong.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.prompt: If you were Safiya, what would you do?
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.image.alt: A woman looking at her phone while her husband sits alone in another room.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.choices.cha: Keep asking what is wrong until he tells me.
Each question feels to Bilal like pressure to perform being okay. He gets quieter. His quietness makes Safiya more frightened, so she asks more. The loop has begun.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.choices.mir: Go quiet too — if he wants space, he can have it.
Now both are withdrawn and each reads the other’s silence as rejection. Days pass and nobody knows how to restart.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-quiet.choices.nam: "You seem drained. I’m here when you want to talk — no rush."
There is nothing to defend against. That evening Bilal sits beside her and, slowly, tells her about work.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.title: Now you are Bilal
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.image.alt: A tired husband in a dim study, his wife's shadow at the door.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.body: You are overwhelmed and need quiet. Safiya has asked three times today if you are okay. You feel crowded.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.choices.shu: Say "I’m fine" and go to another room.
“Fine” with a closed door tells her something is wrong and that she is shut out. Her anxiety spikes. The loop tightens.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.choices.sna: She hears that her care is a burden. She may stop asking — and start silently keeping score.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-space.choices.ret: "Work has wiped me out. I need tonight to recharge — can we talk properly tomorrow after Fajr?"
Space with a return time is completely different from disappearing. She knows what is happening and when you will come back. She can rest too.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-loop.title: Spotting it mid-argument
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-loop.image.alt: A wife following her husband down a hallway as he turns away.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-loop.body: You are both in it: one following the other from room to room wanting to resolve it now; the other saying “I can’t do this right now.”
Whoever is right should keep going until it is settled.
Pushing a withdrawn person rarely settles anything. It usually ends in a worse thing said, or a slammed door.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-loop.choices.paus: One says, "We’re in the loop. Let’s pause for thirty minutes and come back."
Naming the pattern makes it the shared problem instead of each other. Thirty minutes later, both are calmer and actually listening.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-loop.choices.leav: One leaves the house to cool off without saying for how long.
Cooling off helps; vanishing does not. For the one left behind, the open-ended absence is the hardest part.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.title: How the loop breaks
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.body: The one who pursues is asking “are we okay?”. The one who withdraws is asking “can I breathe?”. Each can answer the other’s question:
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.points.0: Pursuer: reach out once, warmly, and trust the space
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.points.1: Withdrawer: take space, but say why and when you will return
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.points.2: Either one can name it: “I think we are in the loop”
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-insight.points.3: Come back when you said you would — every time
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-talk.prompt: When things feel tense, do you tend to move closer or pull away? What would help you most from the other in that moment?
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-talk.followUps.0: Agree on a word or phrase either of you can use to say “we are in the loop”.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-talk.guide.h-g2.t: Tell each other when you need space and when you will return.
content.lab-rule-three.steps.h-talk.guide.h-g3.t: Either of us can say “we’re in the loop” and we pause for thirty minutes.
content.quiz-know-me.title: How well do you know me?
content.quiz-know-me.tagline: Take turns: one answers, the other guesses.
content.quiz-know-me.description: On each card one of you answers about yourself and the other guesses. You swap every card. Keep score if you like — the stories behind the misses are the best part.
content.quiz-know-me.cover.alt: Two hands holding cards face down.
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-comfort.prompt: Your perfect comfort food after a long day?
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-comfort.guessPromp: What is {{name}}’s comfort food after a long day?
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-morning.options.2: Start the day — gym, work, plans
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-hurt.prompt: When you are upset, you mostly want…
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-hurt.guessPrompt: When {{name}} is upset, they mostly want…
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-hurt.talk: Worth remembering for real: this is the card that saves arguments.
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-trip.options.0: Umrah, then a slow tour of Madinah
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-trip.options.3: A beach with nothing to do
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-gift.prompt: Which would mean the most to you?
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-gift.guessPrompt: Which would mean the most to {{name}}?
content.quiz-know-me.cards.km-gift.options.2: Help with something I am dreading

content.adv-first-ramadan.title: The First Ramadan
content.adv-first-ramadan.tagline: Four Fridays, one family iftar, and a comment about samosas.
content.adv-first-ramadan.description: Hamza and Noor are four months married when Ramadan arrives — and Hamza’s mother has plans for it. Take turns as each of them. Small choices early on decide whether Eid feels like a homecoming or a truce.
content.adv-first-ramadan.cover.alt: A young couple preparing a big iftar in a small flat.
content.adv-first-ramadan.roles.A.name: Hamza
content.adv-first-ramadan.roles.A.sketch: Loves his family, hates letting anyone down — especially his mother.
content.adv-first-ramadan.roles.B.name: Noor
content.adv-first-ramadan.roles.B.sketch: Works full-time and hoped for a quiet Ramadan focused on worship.
content.adv-first-ramadan.variables.closeness.re: Hamza and Noor feel far apart.
content.adv-first-ramadan.variables.resentment.r: A few things are still unspoken.
content.adv-first-ramadan.variables.family.label: Family warmth

content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.invite.title: The phone call
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.invite.image.al: Hamza on the phone in the hallway while Noor unpacks shopping.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.invite.passages: Two days before Ramadan, Hamza’s mother calls. “Your first Ramadan as a married couple! The whole family will come to yours for iftar — every Friday. Your new flat, Noor’s cooking. It will be beautiful.”
Noor is in the kitchen. She works full-time, and last week she said she wanted this Ramadan to be quiet: more Qur’an, more tarawih, fewer gatherings.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.invite.decision: You are Hamza. What do you say to your mother?
Hamza agreed to four Friday iftars without asking Noor.
Saying yes for two people is a decision about your spouse’s time — made without them.
“That’s kind, Mum. Let me talk to Noor and call you back tonight.”
Hamza told his mother he would check with Noor first.
“How about one Friday to start? Noor’s working all month.”
Hamza offered his mother one Friday instead of four — before asking Noor.
Noor reading the family group chat at night.
That evening, the family WhatsApp group lights up. “Can’t wait for Fridays at Hamza and Noor’s!” Hearts. A sister-in-law asks what Noor will be making.
Noor scrolls back. Hamza has not said a word to her about it.
This could be a five-minute conversation tonight — or a story Noor tells herself for a month.
You are Noor. What do you do?
“I found out from the group chat. Can we talk about how this was decided?”
Noor raised it with Hamza that same evening, calmly.
Raised early and gently, a small hurt stays small.
Say nothing. It is his family; she will manage.
Noor said nothing and decided to cope.
Notice how a small issue is becoming resentment. Coping quietly is not the same as being okay.
Reply in the group: “Lovely of someone to tell me 🙂”
Noor replied in the family group with a pointed message.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.group_fallout.i: Hamza on an upsetting call from his mother.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.group_fallout.p: The group goes silent. Then Hamza’s mother calls him, upset. “Does your wife not want us there? I was only trying to make her feel welcome.”
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.group_fallout.d: You are Hamza. What do you say?
“Noor should have been asked. That was my mistake, Mum, not hers.”
Hamza took responsibility with his mother instead of blaming Noor.
Owning your part protects your spouse and lowers everyone’s temperature.
Apologise to his mother, then tell Noor she embarrassed him.
Hamza apologised to his mother and told Noor she had embarrassed him.
Noor’s hurt about being left out has now been replaced by a new one: being blamed for it.
Hamza smoothed it over with his mother and talked to nobody.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.talk_plan.title: Kitchen table
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.talk_plan.image: Hamza and Noor planning Ramadan over tea.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.talk_plan.passa: Hamza and Noor sit down with two cups of tea and a calendar.
Hamza has already offered his mother one Friday. Noor notices she was not asked — but at least it is only one.
The group-chat message still hangs between them, but they are here, talking.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.talk_plan.lesso: You both have to pick the same answer. If you don’t, talk it through and choose again.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.talk_plan.decis: Together: how many family iftars will you host this Ramadan?
All four Fridays — it matters to his family.
They agreed to host all four Fridays.
Two Fridays, and alternate the others with Noor’s family.
They agreed on two Fridays, alternating with Noor’s family.
One big iftar, and visit them on other evenings.
They agreed on one big iftar and visits on other nights.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.first_friday.im: A crowded iftar where an older woman comments on the food.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.first_friday.pa: Fourteen people in a flat built for four. Noor left work early and has been cooking since three.
She is exhausted. She has said nothing about the four Fridays, to anyone.
Since the group message, the aunties are polite to Noor — a little too polite.
As the samosas go round, Hamza’s mother laughs: “In our family we make them fresh, not from the freezer. Never mind — Noor will learn!” A few people laugh along.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.first_friday.le: You each decide what your character does — at the same moment, without knowing what the other will do.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.first_friday.de: In that moment, what do you do?
Laugh along to keep the mood light.
Hamza laughed along at the comment.
This response may make your partner feel dismissed — and alone in a room full of family.
“Honestly, Noor’s samosas are the best I’ve had. Pass them here!”
Hamza warmly praised Noor’s food in front of everyone.
Say nothing now; plan to speak to his mother privately.
Hamza let the moment pass, planning to speak to his mother privately.
Noor smiled and swallowed the comment.
“Next year you’ll have to teach me, Khala!”
Noor answered with a light joke that invited her mother-in-law in.
Excuse herself to the kitchen to cool down.
Noor left the room to cool down.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.warm_kitchen.im: Noor and her mother-in-law laughing at the sink.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.warm_kitchen.pa: Later, Hamza’s mother finds Noor washing up. “You know, my mother-in-law said the same to me about my dal. I cried for a week.” They both laugh.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.warm_kitchen.de: “Come early next Friday and we’ll make them fresh together.”
Noor invited her mother-in-law to cook with her.
Thank her warmly, and keep hosting her own way.
Noor thanked her mother-in-law and kept hosting her own way.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.tarawih_quiet.i: A silent drive to tarawih at night.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.tarawih_quiet.p: They drive to tarawih in silence. Noor stares out of the window. Hamza can feel something is wrong but cannot name it.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.tarawih_quiet.l: When both people swallow the same moment, it does not disappear. It waits.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.tarawih_quiet.d: You are Hamza. What do you do?
“You’ve gone quiet. Was it something tonight?”
Hamza noticed Noor’s silence and asked about it.
Put on Qur’an recitation and say nothing.
Hamza filled the silence with recitation instead of a question.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.after_iftar.ima: Hamza and Noor in the kitchen after guests leave.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.after_iftar.pas: Midnight. The flat is quiet again, the sink full.
Noor keeps hearing the laughter — and Hamza’s laugh among it.
Hamza’s words — “the best I’ve had” — are still making her smile.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.after_iftar.dec: You are Noor. What do you do?
“Can I tell you how the samosa comment felt?”
Noor told Hamza calmly how the comment felt.
“I’m fine. Just tired.” And go to sleep.
Noor said she was fine and went to sleep.
Let it all out: the WhatsApp, the four Fridays, the laughing.
Noor let out everything she had been holding in, all at once.
A month of small things just arrived as one big thing. Hamza will hear it as an attack.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.hamza_listens.p: Noor explains: in front of everyone, after cooking for hours, it felt like being graded.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.hamza_listens.d: You are Hamza. What do you say first?
“That’s just how Mum is. She doesn’t mean anything by it.”
Hamza explained his mother instead of hearing Noor.
Explaining before acknowledging tells your spouse their feelings are the problem.
“That sounds like it really hurt. What would help?”
Hamza acknowledged Noor’s hurt and asked what would help.
Validation does not necessarily mean agreement. Hamza can love his mother and still say Noor’s feelings make sense.
“I’ll talk to Mum tomorrow. You shouldn’t have to deal with that.”
Hamza promised to speak to his mother himself.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.mum_conversatio: Hamza talking with his mother at her kitchen table.
After suhoor, Hamza visits his mother. She pours tea. He has rehearsed this three times.
You are Hamza. How do you put it?
“Noor was really upset about what you said.”
Hamza told his mother Noor was upset — making Noor the complainant.
Carrying the complaint as hers puts Noor between him and his mother.
“I want Noor to feel at home with us, Mum. Comments like that make it hard — for me too.”
Hamza set a boundary with his mother in his own voice.
Lose his nerve and talk about the weather.
Hamza lost his nerve and never raised it.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.blowup.title: Everything at once
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.blowup.image.al: Noor letting everything out as Hamza stands stunned.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.blowup.passages: It pours out — the group chat, the Fridays, the laughing, the exhaustion. Hamza stands in the kitchen doorway, stunned. He did not know any of this.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.blowup.decision: You are Hamza. What do you do?
“You agreed to all of this! Why didn’t you say anything?”
Hamza defended himself against the flood.
Go quiet and leave the room.
Hamza went quiet and left the room.
An anxious/avoidant loop is forming here: the more she pursues, the more he retreats.
“I didn’t know any of this. We’re both exhausted — can we talk properly after suhoor?”
Hamza asked for a pause with a time to come back.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.cold_week.title: A cold week
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.cold_week.image: Hamza and Noor praying apart in a cold silence.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.cold_week.passa: The last ten nights begin. They are polite. They pray in the same masjid and drive home without speaking.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.cold_week.lesso: Each of you decides privately what you would do now.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.cold_week.decis: What do you do this week?
One of them reached out first.
Wait for them to come to you.
One of them waited to be reached.
Make du’a for the two of you, every night.
One of them made du’a for the marriage every night.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.one_sided.title: An olive branch
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.one_sided.image: A cup of tea offered as a peace gesture.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.one_sided.passa: A cup of tea appears on the other’s side of the table. A small, awkward offering.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.one_sided.decis: Together: what happens with the olive branch?
They accepted the olive branch and talked.
Take it — but keep things light. No deep talk.
They made peace on the surface and left the rest unsaid.
content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.laylatul_qadr.i: Hamza and Noor walking home together late at night.

content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.boundary_plan.t: A plan for the two of you

content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.boundary_plan.d: Together: what will you do for the rest of Ramadan?
Keep hosting — and Hamza answers comments in the moment.

content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.last_ten.title: The last ten nights

content.adv-first-ramadan.scenes.last_ten.decisi: How do you spend the last ten nights?

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.imag: Both families at one long Eid table.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.patt: Each time something hurt, someone eventually named it — and the other heard it.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.coul: Very little — though deciding the Fridays together from the start would have spared them the hardest week.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.take: Families blend when the couple acts as a team first.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.epil: Next Ramadan, Hamza calls Noor before he answers his mother.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.one_table.guid: We decide together before we say yes to family plans.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.im: Hamza and Noor praying side by side at home.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.wh: Hamza and Noor end the month with fewer gatherings than his family hoped for — and a closeness neither expected.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.pa: Hurts were raised while they were still small, so they stayed small.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.co: Including the family a little more might have kept everyone warmer without costing the two of them anything.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.ta: A marriage needs its own rhythm, even inside a big family.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.our_ramadan.ep: Hamza’s mother is a little cool for a while.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.cracks.title: Cracks under the lanterns

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.cracks.whatHap: Eid looks perfect in the photos. At home, Hamza and Noor barely speak.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.cracks.pattern: Nothing big happened. Many small things went unsaid until they became a wall.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.cracks.takeawa: Silence keeps the peace for a day and costs it for a month.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.cracks.epilogu: Hamza still doesn’t fully understand what went wrong.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.us_against_the: Hamza and Noor alone at Eid breakfast, a phone ignored.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.polite_truce.i: Hamza and Noor exchanging gifts politely.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.polite_truce.p: They stopped the conflict without understanding it, so it will return in a new form.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.polite_truce.c: Using the olive branch to have the real conversation, not to avoid it.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.polite_truce.t: An argument ended is not the same as an argument resolved.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.polite_truce.g: When we make peace, we also talk about what happened.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.imag: Hamza and Noor getting ready for Eid in separate rooms.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.what: Both waited for the other to move first. Eid comes and goes with polite greetings and nothing more.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.patt: When both people withdraw, nobody is left to start the repair.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.coul: Either one of them reaching out — it did not matter who.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.take: Waiting to be reached is a choice too.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.quiet_eid.guid: Whoever notices the distance first reaches out first.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.i: Hamza and Noor sharing sweets on a balcony after Eid.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.w: Some evenings were hard and some were lovely. They end the month tired, a little wiser, and still on the same side.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.p: They handled some moments well and others not — and noticed the difference.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.c: Talking sooner about what each of them wanted from Ramadan, before the family plans began.
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.t: Before a big season, ask each other: what do you hope this will feel like?
content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.e: Something small is still unsaid between them.

content.adv-first-ramadan.endings.steady_start.g: Before Ramadan and Eid, we talk about what we each hope for.
Noor and her mother-in-law folding samosas together.

content.adv-read-at-1142.title: Read at 11:42
content.adv-read-at-1142.tagline: One message. Five hours of silence. A liked photo.
content.adv-read-at-1142.description: Yusuf is away for a week on a work trip. Maryam’s message shows “read” — and no reply. Play both sides of a week where a bad day, a phone and two different ways of coping can draw a couple closer or start a loop neither can stop.
content.adv-read-at-1142.cover.alt: A phone on a bedside table showing an unanswered message.
content.adv-read-at-1142.roles.A.name: Yusuf
content.adv-read-at-1142.roles.A.sketch: Goes quiet when he is stressed. Thinks of it as protecting her from his mood.
content.adv-read-at-1142.roles.B.name: Maryam
content.adv-read-at-1142.roles.B.sketch: Feels distance quickly. Reaches out when she senses it.
content.adv-read-at-1142.variables.trust.label: Trust
content.adv-read-at-1142.variables.loop.label: The loop
content.adv-read-at-1142.variables.loop.readings: The loop flickers now and then.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_message.imag: Maryam glancing at an unanswered message at work.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_message.pass: Eight months married. Yusuf is in Manchester for a week of client meetings. At 11:40 Maryam sends: “How did the big presentation go? 🤍”
Read, 11:42. Then nothing. One hour. Three hours. Five.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_message.deci: You are Maryam. What do you do?
Maryam sent a second, more anxious message.
Assume he is busy and get on with her day.
Maryam assumed he was busy and got on with her day.
Open Instagram to see if he has been online.
Maryam went looking for signs of him online.
Searching for evidence when anxious tends to find some — whether or not it means anything.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_like.title: The like
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_like.image.a: Maryam looking at a liked photo on her phone.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_like.passage: There it is. Forty minutes ago, Yusuf liked a photo — a former colleague’s graduation picture. She is smiling in her gown.
He has time for that, but not for her?
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_like.decisio: Send him the screenshot: “So you DO have time.”
Maryam sent Yusuf a screenshot of the like with an accusation.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.yusuf_meeting.im: Yusuf alone in a stairwell, staring at his phone.

Space with a return time is completely different from disappearing.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.silent_evening.i: Yusuf and Maryam awake in separate cities.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.silent_evening.l: Each of you decides what your character does tonight, without knowing what the other is doing.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.evening_call.ima: Maryam listening to Yusuf on the phone.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_like_talk.im: Yusuf and Maryam on a difficult phone call.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.jealousy_fork.im: Maryam alone on the kitchen floor, thinking.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.jealousy_fork.pa: Silence on the line. Maryam can feel the conversation slipping.
content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.jealousy_fork.de: You are Maryam. What do you do?

“If there’s nothing to hide, give me your passwords.”

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.sweet_unsaid.ima: Yusuf and Maryam enjoying a weekend walk.

content.adv-read-at-1142.scenes.the_talk.title: The talk

They agreed together what feels respectful online.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.return_time.ima: Maryam smiling at a message saying “back at 9”.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.return_time.wha: Next trip, Yusuf has another bad day. He sends: “Rough one. Need an hour. Back at nine.” At nine, he calls. Maryam barely notices the hour.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.return_time.pat: He learned to take space with a return time; she learned to trust the space.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.return_time.cou: Not much now — but the first silence could have been one two-minute call.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.return_time.tak: Space is safe when it comes with a return.

content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.ima: Two phones side by side, ignored, as the couple share tea.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.wha: They agree what feels respectful online. The like stops mattering — because neither of them has to guess anymore.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.pat: The photo was never the problem. Feeling unseen was.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.cou: Maryam asking about the photo calmly, rather than searching first.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.tak: Agree your boundaries before you need them.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.open_phones.gui: We agree together what feels respectful online.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.title: One line

content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.whatHa: The one-line rule works. Not perfectly — Yusuf forgets twice — but the silence never stretches to five hours again.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.patter: A tiny, concrete agreement prevented the gap where anxiety grows.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.couldH: Talking about why Yusuf goes quiet, not just what to do about it.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.takeaw: The smallest agreements are the ones you actually keep.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.one_line.epilog: The loop still flickers when he is stressed.

content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.title: The loop wins
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.image: Two figures on a circular staircase, never meeting.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.whatH: Each trip, the same pattern: his silence, her calls, his retreat, her panic. They love each other and keep hurting each other the same way.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.patte: Each one’s coping move triggered the other’s, again and again.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.could: Either of them naming the pattern out loud, once, instead of fighting inside it.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.takea: You can’t fix a loop by doing your half harder.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.loop_wins.guide: When we notice the loop, we name it and pause — together.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.im: A phone lying between Yusuf and Maryam at dinner.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.wh: Yusuf hands over his passwords. Maryam finds nothing. Somehow they both feel worse.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.pa: Checking soothes anxiety for an hour and erodes trust for months.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.co: Saying the feeling underneath — “I felt invisible” — instead of asking for proof.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.ta: Access is not the same as trust.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.surveillance.gu: We talk about what we feel instead of checking each other’s phones.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.next_trip.title: Next month

content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.next_trip.patte: Peace was kept by not talking, so nothing changed.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.next_trip.could: One honest conversation before the next trip.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.next_trip.takea: What isn’t talked about tends to repeat.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.next_trip.guide: We talk about a hard week before the next one starts.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.title: Closer than before
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.image.al: Yusuf and Maryam asleep on the sofa after talking.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.whatHapp: The bad week becomes the week they understood each other: why he goes quiet, why she reaches out.

content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.couldHav: Writing down one agreement would help it last.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.takeaway: Behind most reactions is a fear. Ask about the fear.
content.adv-read-at-1142.endings.closer.guide.m-: When the other reacts strongly, we ask what they were afraid of.
Yusuf and Maryam on their phones, a gap between them.

Any one moment of turning toward: one call, one honest message, one question asked kindly.

We turn toward each other’s small bids for attention.
Yusuf and Maryam walking by a canal, talking.

content.adv-the-offer.title: The Offer
content.adv-the-offer.tagline: A dream job in Dubai. A father who isn’t well. One decision for two.
content.adv-the-offer.description: Hana is offered the role of her career — in Dubai, starting in three months. Idris’s father had a stroke last year. Play both of them through a decision about careers, money, family and where home is. Every path has a cost; the question is who chooses it.
content.adv-the-offer.cover.alt: Hana holding a job offer letter while Idris looks at a family photo.
content.adv-the-offer.roles.A.name: Idris
content.adv-the-offer.roles.A.sketch: An only son. Proud of Hana, worried about his father.
content.adv-the-offer.roles.B.name: Hana
content.adv-the-offer.roles.B.sketch: Has worked towards this kind of role for eight years.
content.adv-the-offer.variables.partnership.read: They made it as two separate people.
content.adv-the-offer.variables.family.label: Family ties
The family feels honoured and included.
content.adv-the-offer.variables.fulfilment.label: Hana’s fulfilment
content.adv-the-offer.variables.fulfilment.readi: Hana feels she gave up something of herself.
Hana is at peace with how it went.
Hana feels she is becoming who she hoped to be.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.the_email.title: The email
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.the_email.image.alt: Hana reading a job offer email in surprise.
Tuesday, 10pm. Hana opens the email: Head of Product, Dubai. Twice her salary. Start in three months.
She applied on a whim. She never expected to get it. Idris is downstairs, on the phone to his father, who had a stroke last year and is still recovering.
You are Hana. What do you do?
Run downstairs and tell Idris straight away.
Hana told Idris about the offer the moment she saw it.
Keep it to herself for a few days to think.
Hana kept the offer to herself for a few days.
Thinking first is reasonable. The risk is that someone else tells him before you do.
Hana declined the offer that night without telling Idris.
A sacrifice your spouse never knew about is one they can’t appreciate — or question.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_reacts.title: Downstairs
Idris reacting as Hana shares the news.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_reacts.passag: Idris hangs up with his father as Hana appears in the doorway, holding her laptop, eyes shining.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_reacts.decisi: You are Idris. What is your first reaction?
Idris’s first words were about his father.
His worry is real — but leading with it means Hana’s joy went unheard.
Idris said “we’ll see” and went quiet.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_finds.title: At her parents’ dinner
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_finds.image.a: Idris hearing the news from Hana's sister at dinner.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_finds.passage: Saturday dinner at Hana’s parents. Her sister beams at Idris: “Dubai! You must be so proud!” Idris smiles. He has no idea what she means.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.idris_finds.decisio: You are Idris. What do you do?
Wait until home: “I heard about Dubai tonight. I wish I’d heard it from you.”
Idris waited until they were home and raised it gently.
In the car: “Why am I the last to know?”
Idris confronted Hana in the car.
Say nothing, and feel quietly hurt.
Idris said nothing and nursed the hurt.
A hurt kept quiet tends to come out sideways — usually in the decision itself.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.quiet_regret.title: Three weeks later
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.quiet_regret.passag: Hana has been flat for weeks. One evening she mentions, almost in passing: “I was offered a job in Dubai. I said no.”
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.quiet_regret.decisi: You are Idris. What do you say?
“You turned it down without telling me? Is there still time to talk about it?”
Idris asked whether it was too late to decide together.
“That means a lot. Thank you for putting family first.”
Idris thanked Hana for her sacrifice and let it rest.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.first_talk.title: What matters most
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.first_talk.image.al: Idris and Hana each writing privately on a card.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.first_talk.passages: They sit down to talk properly. Before they start, Hana suggests they each write down, privately, what matters most to them.
The company has agreed to hold the role for a month while she reconsiders.
Choose for your own character. You will both see the cards at once.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.first_talk.decision: Idris wrote: being here for my father.
Our savings and our future children.
Idris wrote: our savings and our future.
Idris wrote: Hana getting to do this.
This chance — it may not come again.
Hana wrote: this chance may not come again.
Hana wrote: staying near our families.
Hana wrote: whatever Idris truly wants.
Idris and Hana each insisting on the other's wish.
“You should take it.” “No — your dad.” “But it’s your dream.” Neither will choose for themselves.
Together: how do you get unstuck?
Write out every option, however unlikely.
They wrote out every option together.
Both pray istikhara and set a date to decide.
They both prayed istikhara and set a date to decide.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.family_hears.title: His mother calls
Idris on the phone with his mother while Hana watches.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.family_hears.passag: Somehow, Idris’s mother has heard. She calls him, crying. “You can’t take my only son away while your father is like this.”
He is still hurt that he heard about Dubai from Hana’s sister.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.family_hears.decisi: You are Idris. What do you tell his mother?
“It’s a decision Hana and I will make together, Mum — and we’ll think about you and Dad in it.”
Idris told his mother it was a decision for him and Hana to make together.
Including family in your thinking is different from handing them the decision.
“Don’t worry, Mum. We’re not going anywhere.”
Idris promised his mother they would not go — before deciding with Hana.
“It’s Hana’s job, Mum, not my idea.”
Idris told his mother the whole thing was Hana’s idea.
Putting it on Hana keeps him safe with his mother and sets his wife against her.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.hana_learns.title: Hana hears
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.hana_learns.image.a: Hana stunned by a call from her mother-in-law.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.hana_learns.passage: Hana’s mother-in-law calls her. “Thank you for staying, dear. Idris told me.”
Hana’s mother-in-law messages her: “I hope you’ll think about what you’re asking of my son.”
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.hana_learns.decisio: You are Hana. What do you do?
“I need us to decide together before anyone else is told anything.”
Hana asked calmly that they decide together before telling anyone.
“So your mother decides our life now?”
Hana accused Idris of letting his mother decide.
Say nothing. Let it go. Resent it quietly.
Hana accepted it without a word and resented it.
Notice how a decision is becoming resentment. Silent agreement isn’t agreement.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.options.title: The options
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.options.image.alt: Four option cards laid out on a table.
The options are on the table. None of them is free.
Both of them prayed istikhara this week. Neither feels certain, but both feel calmer.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.options.decision.ch: Go to Dubai for two years, with a review after one.
They chose two years in Dubai with a review after one.
Go — and use the extra income for his father’s care and frequent visits.
They chose Dubai and to fund his father’s care and regular visits.
Stay — Hana negotiates a hybrid version of the role.
They chose to stay and try to negotiate a hybrid role.
They chose to stay and decline.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.negotiation.title: The counter-offer
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.negotiation.image.a: Hana negotiating on a video call.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.negotiation.passage: The company is interested but cautious: “We could do London-based, with one week a month in Dubai.”
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.negotiation.decisio: You are Hana. What do you do?
Take it — one week a month.
Hana accepted a London role with monthly trips.
Push for fully remote, with Idris’s support behind her.
With Idris behind her, Hana negotiated a fully remote role.
Walk away — half a dream feels worse than none.
Hana walked away from the counter-offer.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.title: Six months in
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.image.alt: Idris on a video call with his father from a Dubai balcony.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.passages.0.te: Dubai is bright and busy. Hana is thriving. Then the call: Idris’s father has had a fall.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.passages.1.te: The carers they pay for found him quickly. He is shaken, not badly hurt.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.decision.prom: What do you each think should happen?
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai.decision.choi: Idris flies back for a month.
One of them wanted Idris to fly back for a month.
We all go home, for good.
One of them wanted to go home for good.
More care for him; we visit more often.
One of them wanted more care and more visits.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_strain.title: Guilt
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_strain.passag: Idris is working late more often. He doesn’t say why. Hana suspects she knows.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_strain.decisi: You are Idris. What do you do?
“I feel guilty every day we’re here. I need you to know that.”
Idris told Hana about his guilt.
Keep it to himself and work longer hours.
Idris buried his guilt in work.
Guilt left unsaid often turns into distance — or blame.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_settles.title: A rhythm
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_settles.image: Idris and Hana on a happy call with his father.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_settles.passa: Idris spends a month at home. His father improves. They find a rhythm: calls every evening, visits every few months.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.dubai_settles.decis: You are Hana. What do you do?
Offer to drop to four days a week so visits are easier.
Hana offered to work four days so they could visit more.
Keep going at full speed — this is the window.
Hana kept going at full speed.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.homecoming.title: Home
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.homecoming.image.al: A family reunion at the airport.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.homecoming.passages: They fly home with eleven boxes and a lot of feelings. Idris’s father cries at the airport.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.homecoming.decision: You are Hana. How do you handle it?
Throw herself into finding a new role at home.
Hana threw herself into finding a new role.
Tell Idris honestly that she is grieving the job.
Hana told Idris honestly that she was grieving the job.
Choosing something together doesn’t mean neither of you lost anything.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.staying.title: Staying
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.staying.image.alt: Idris helping his father walk as Hana works nearby.
They stay. Idris’s father slowly gets stronger.
Hana still thinks about the email at least once a day.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.staying.decision.pr: You are Idris. What do you do?
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.staying.decision.ch: Take on more of his father’s care, so Hana can push her career here.
Idris took on more of his father’s care so Hana could grow her career.
Assume Hana will help with the visits too, as before.
Idris assumed Hana would carry the visits as before.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.year_later.title: One year later
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.year_later.image.al: Idris and Hana on a bench a year later.
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.year_later.passages: A year since the email. One evening, Hana asks: “Can we talk about how this year has really been?”
content.adv-the-offer.scenes.year_later.decision: Together: do you look back honestly?
Yes — properly, including what it cost each of you.
A year on, they looked back honestly at what it had cost.
Keep the peace. It’s done; why reopen it?
A year on, they chose not to look back.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.the_promise.title: The promise
Hana at a rainy window, the old offer pinned behind her.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.the_promise.whatHa: They stayed because Idris promised his mother before he asked his wife. Hana has never quite forgiven the order it happened in.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.the_promise.patter: A shared decision was made by one person and a parent — the spouse was informed, not consulted.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.the_promise.couldH: Idris saying to his mother: “Hana and I will decide this together.” The outcome might have been the same; the marriage would not.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.the_promise.takeaw: How a decision is made matters as much as what is decided.
We make major decisions together before telling family.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.title: Both, and
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.image.alt: Idris’s father laughing on a video call with the couple.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.whatHappe: Hana’s career grows, Idris’s father is cared for and close, and the decision belongs to both of them.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.pattern.e: They put every option on the table, listened to each other’s fears, and chose together.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.couldHave: Little. The hardest days were the early ones, before they started talking as a team.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.takeaway: The answer is often not either/or, once you stop deciding alone.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.epilogues: Idris’s mother now tells everyone about “my daughter-in-law in Dubai”.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.both_and.guide.o-e: For big decisions, we lay out every option before choosing.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.ima: Idris alone in an office at night beside a family photo.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.wha: Dubai is going well on paper. Idris carries a guilt he has never put into words, and it is turning into distance.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.pat: An unspoken feeling did not go away; it went underground.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.cou: Idris saying, once, “I feel guilty every day we are here.”
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.tak: Feelings you don’t share still shape the marriage — you just can’t see how.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.distance_guilt.gui: We say the hard feeling out loud, even when the decision is made.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.title: Home again
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.image.a: A family lunch at home, with moving boxes in the corner.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.whatHap: They came back for his father. The family is whole again. Hana gave up something real.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.pattern: The choice was right for the family — and still a loss for Hana.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.couldHa: Naming that loss together, so it does not become a debt.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.takeawa: A sacrifice is lighter when it is seen and shared.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.epilogu: Hana and Idris talk about it openly. It stings less each month.
Nobody has asked Hana how she feels about it.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.home_again.guide.o: When one of us gives something up, we name it and honour it.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.ima: Hana walking a road, glancing back at the other path.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.wha: Life is good and steady. But Hana feels she gave up a piece of who she was going to be — and isn’t sure Idris knows.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.pat: When one spouse quietly gives something up, it can become an invisible debt.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.cou: Deciding out loud and together — even if they still stayed.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.tak: Don’t sacrifice in secret. Let your spouse share the cost.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.road_not_taken.gui: Neither of us makes a big sacrifice in secret.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.separate_decisions: Idris and Hana working back to back in their kitchen.
Each of them made their own moves — with family, with work, alone. They live in the result together, but neither feels it was theirs.
They acted as two individuals managing a situation, not a couple facing one.
Sitting down early, writing down what mattered, and deciding as one.
A marriage is a shared decision-maker — or it becomes two roommates.
Big decisions are ours, not mine or yours.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.title: A new shape
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.image.al: Hana working from home with a boarding pass, Idris bringing tea.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.whatHapp: Not the job as offered — a new version of it. Hana works from London with trips to Dubai. It is not perfect, but it is theirs.
Instead of choosing between two options, they made a third.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.couldHav: Asking for the hybrid version sooner, before the family pressure built.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.takeaway: When both choices hurt someone, look for the one nobody has offered yet.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.new_shape.guide.o-: When we’re stuck between two options, we look for a third.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.i: Idris and Hana holding hands across a café table.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.w: Not everyone is happy with what they chose. But Idris and Hana both know it was their decision, made together.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.p: Because both had a real voice, neither carries the decision alone.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.c: Bringing the families in more gently might have eased the pressure.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.t: Make the decision together, and you can carry its cost together.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.e: Every year on the date of the email, they review the decision over dinner.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.decided_together.g: We review big decisions together after a year.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.ima: Idris and Hana walking by a river at sunset.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.wha: The year went the way it went — some of it chosen, some of it simply happening. They are still talking about what it meant.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.pat: Some of the decision was shared; some was left to circumstance and family.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.cou: More honesty early about what each of them truly wanted.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.tak: Say what you want before you say what you will settle for.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.epi: They never did talk about what the year cost them.
content.adv-the-offer.endings.still_deciding.gui: We say what we actually want before we compromise.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.title: Fajr Alarm
content.adv-fajr-alarm.tagline: One prays every prayer at the masjid. One is just trying to keep up.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.description: Zaid has found his way back to the masjid and prays every prayer there. Amal prays too — but Fajr after night shifts is a struggle, and lately she feels watched in her own home. Play both of them through a season where encouragement and judgement look very alike.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.cover.alt: A man unrolling a prayer mat before dawn as his wife sleeps.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.roles.A.name: Zaid
content.adv-fajr-alarm.roles.A.sketch: Newly devoted, full of energy, wants to share it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.roles.B.name: Amal
content.adv-fajr-alarm.roles.B.sketch: A nurse on night shifts; prays, but Fajr is her hardest prayer.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.variables.closeness.label: Closeness
content.adv-fajr-alarm.variables.closeness.readi: They feel watched rather than seen.
They feel deeply on each other’s side.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.variables.judgement.label: Judgement in the home
content.adv-fajr-alarm.variables.judgement.readi: Their home feels free of judgement.
Some pressure hangs in the air.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.variables.faith.label: Shared faith
Worship has become something they do apart.
They each keep their own practice.
Faith has become something they share.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.title: 5:02 a.m.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.image.alt: Zaid silencing the alarm while Amal sleeps.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.passages.0.t: Zaid’s alarm goes off for Fajr. For the last three months he has not missed a single prayer at the masjid, and he has never felt closer to Allah.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.passages.1.t: Amal got home from a twelve-hour night shift at one. She is fast asleep.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.decision.pro: You are Zaid. What do you do?
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.alarm.decision.cho: Zaid woke Amal for Fajr after her night shift.
Encouragement that ignores how someone is doing can feel like supervision.
Let her sleep — and ask later how she’d like Fajr to work.
Zaid let Amal sleep and resolved to ask her how she wanted Fajr to work.
Pray alone, and quietly hope she’ll join one day.
Zaid prayed alone and kept his hopes to himself.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.title: Breakfast
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.image.alt: Zaid and Amal talking over a late breakfast.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.passages.0: Late morning. Amal pads into the kitchen.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.passages.1: “You woke me at five,” she says, before he can say good morning.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.passages.2: Zaid mentions, lightly, that he’d love them to pray Fajr together one day.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.decision.p: You are Amal. What do you say?
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.morning.decision.c: Tell him honestly how hard Fajr is after nights, and that she does pray it — late.
Amal told Zaid honestly how hard Fajr was after night shifts.
Amal snapped that she was not a child.
Promise to try — then hit snooze every morning.
Amal promised to try and quietly kept snoozing.
Agreeing to keep the peace postpones the conversation — and adds guilt to it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.friend_visit.title: A friend at the door
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.friend_visit.image: Zaid’s friend making a remark in the doorway.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.friend_visit.passa: After Maghrib, Zaid’s friend from the masjid drops by. At the door he smiles: “We never see Sister Amal at Fajr, akhi. Bring her along!”
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.friend_visit.decis: You are Zaid. What do you say?
Zaid told his friend Amal’s worship was between her and Allah.
Laugh awkwardly and change the subject.
Zaid laughed it off without answering.
Zaid told his friend he was “working on” Amal.
Talking about a spouse as a project — even kindly — turns partnership into supervision.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.overheard.title: Overheard
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.overheard.image.al: Amal overhearing the conversation in the hall.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.overheard.passages: Amal heard every word from the kitchen.
“That’s between Amal and Allah.” Something in her chest unclenches.
“Working on her.” She puts the dish down very carefully.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.overheard.decision: You are Amal. What do you do?
After the guest leaves, sit Zaid down and talk properly.
Amal sat Zaid down for a proper conversation.
Say nothing. Pray in her room, alone, from now on.
Amal withdrew and began praying alone, out of sight.
Start going to Fajr — mostly so nobody can say anything.
Amal began going to Fajr mainly to stop the comments.
Worship done for an audience can quietly empty it of meaning.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.title: The kitchen table
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.image.alt: Zaid and Amal talking at the kitchen table.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.passages.0.te: They sit with two cups of tea. For once, nobody is trying to win.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.lessons.fa-l-: Choose together. If you pick differently, talk it through and choose again.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.decision.prom: Together: how will worship work in your home?
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.talk.decision.choi: Pray together when we can — never as pressure.
They agreed to pray together when they could, without pressure.
Zaid wakes her only on days she asks.
They agreed Zaid would wake Amal only when she asked.
Each keeps their own practice, privately.
They agreed to keep worship private to each of them.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.distance.title: Separate rooms, separate mats
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.distance.image.alt: Zaid and Amal praying in separate rooms.
A week of politeness. Two prayer mats, two rooms.
What do you do this week?
Make du’a for the other, quietly.
One of them made quiet du’a for the other.
One of them raised it again.
One of them left it alone.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.title: Ramadan arrives
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.image.alt: Zaid and Amal preparing suhoor before dawn.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.passages.0: Ramadan begins. Suhoor at four, and Amal is on nights for the first week.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.passages.1: Amal has been going to Fajr every day. She has never felt further from it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.decision.p: What do you hope this Ramadan looks like?
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.ramadan.decision.b: Ask Amal what she wants from Ramadan.
Zaid asked Amal what she wanted from Ramadan.
Plan a suhoor-and-Fajr routine for both of them.
Zaid planned a routine for both of them.
Spend every night at the masjid.
Zaid spent every night at the masjid.
Suggest a small shared goal — a juz together each week.
Amal suggested reading a juz together each week.
Join him for suhoor and Fajr when she can.
Amal joined him for suhoor and Fajr when she could.
Keep her own Ramadan, in her own time.
Amal kept her own Ramadan, in her own time.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.lonely.title: Iftar for one
Amal breaks her fast alone again. Zaid will eat at the masjid.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.lonely.decision.pr: You are Amal. What do you do?
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.lonely.decision.ch: Message him: “I miss you at iftar.”
Amal told Zaid she missed him at iftar.
Build her own quiet Ramadan without him.
Amal built a quiet Ramadan without him.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.quiet_night.title: The twenty-seventh night
Zaid and Amal praying together at night.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.quiet_night.passag: The twenty-seventh night. Amal is off work.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.quiet_night.decisi: You are Zaid. What do you do?
Stay home and pray beside her.
Zaid stayed home on the twenty-seventh night to pray beside Amal.
Go to the masjid — but first thank her for her patience with him.
Zaid thanked Amal for her patience before going to the masjid.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.last_night.title: After Eid
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.last_night.image.a: Zaid and Amal reflecting after Eid.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.last_night.passage: Eid is over. The question is what stays.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.scenes.last_night.decisio: Together: what do you keep from this season?
They kept one prayer together every day.
A rule: encouragement only when asked.
They agreed encouragement would come only when asked.
They kept nothing formal, just goodwill.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.title: Growing together
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.image.alt: Zaid and Amal walking home from Fajr together.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.whatHappe: Fajr is still hard after nights. But now, some mornings, Amal wakes Zaid.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.pattern.e: Faith grew once it stopped being measured.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.couldHave: Asking first, from the very first morning.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.takeaway: You cannot drag someone closer to Allah. You can walk beside them.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.epilogues: They finish the Qur’an together by the next Ramadan.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.growing.guide.fa-: We invite each other to worship; we never keep score.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.kindness.title: Only when asked
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.kindness.whatHapp: Zaid stops waking her. Six weeks later, Amal asks him to — on her days off.
Making encouragement opt-in removed the shame from it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.kindness.couldHav: Agreeing this before the friend’s comment would have spared a hard week.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.kindness.takeaway: Encouragement lands when it is welcome.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.kindness.guide.fa: Reminders about worship only when asked for.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.title: Praying for an audience
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.image: Amal at Fajr, present but far away.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.whatH: Amal never misses Fajr now. She has never felt emptier in it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.patte: Pressure produced the behaviour and drained the meaning.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.could: Amal saying how the comment felt — and Zaid listening — instead of performing to end it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.takea: Outward practice without inner peace is worth talking about, not hiding.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.performance.guide: We talk about how worship feels, not just whether it happened.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.title: A scorecard home
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.image.alt: Zaid glancing at the clock while Amal looks away.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.whatHappen: Every prayer has become a test Amal is either passing or failing in Zaid’s eyes.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.pattern.ex: Zeal without gentleness turned a shared faith into supervision.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.couldHaveC: Zaid defending her privacy in front of his friend, and asking rather than waking.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.takeaway: Gentleness is part of the deen, not an exception to it.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.judged.guide.fa-e: We correct each other privately, gently, and rarely.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.title: Parallel prayer mats
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.image.al: Two prayer mats on separate shelves.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.whatHapp: They both pray. They just never do it together, and never talk about it.
Silence kept the peace and lost the shared part of their faith.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.couldHav: Either of them raising it again — it did not matter who.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.takeaway: Faith kept private by default can become faith kept apart.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.parallel.guide.fa: We share something of our worship, even something small.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.title: He took her side
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.whatHapp: Years later, Amal still remembers the night he said “That’s between Amal and Allah.”
Protecting a spouse in front of others built more trust than any conversation.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.couldHav: Little — though speaking about Fajr earlier would have helped.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.takeaway: Defend your spouse in public; discuss in private.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.epilogue: His friend apologises to Amal at Eid.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.defended.guide.fa: We never criticise each other’s deen in front of others.
content.adv-fajr-alarm.endings.one_prayer.title: One prayer a day
Zaid and Amal praying Isha together.
